Everyone knows Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT). It's a retail behemoth, with a recent market value of roughly $1 trillion and some 10,900 stores in 19 countries. It employs about 2.1 million people worldwide and serves some 280 million customers. (With Earth's population of 8 billion people, there's clearly room for growth for Walmart, despite its large size.) Indeed, Walmart is one of Earth's largest employers.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Clearly, the company has been doing well in recent years. (The stock gained 73.5% in 2024 alone!) But all that growth has left the stock rather overvalued, with a recent price-to-sales ratio of 1.37, well above the five-year average of 0.85, and a recent forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 38, well above the five-year average of 27.

Should you invest in Walmart?

So, should you invest in Walmart? I would hold off, as you'd be paying a steep per-share price. The stock will likely continue to grow over the coming decades, but it may also retreat to a more reasonable valuation in the next year or two -- especially if there's a stock market crash.

Think of it this way: The stock was recently priced around $126 per share. If you buy now and it hits $200 in five years, you'll enjoy a roughly 60% gain -- about 10% annually on average. But if you choose to wait, hoping for a better price, and you can snag shares at, say, $100 per share, you'll enjoy a 100% gain when the shares hit $200 (about 15% annualized).

Buying some shares now could serve you well, as long as you're planning to hold for many years. But there are other, less richly valued portfolio candidates out there, too.

Image from Pixabay

Pick up a pack of ground beef this weekend and look at the sticker. In October, beef prices at the store rose 0.9% in a single month, more than twice the 0.4% rise in all consumer prices. Here is the odd part: the company that packs much of that beef is losing money on it. Tyson Foods expected its beef business to lose $625 million to $775 million in the fiscal year that just ended, citing one of the most severe cattle shortages in U.S. history.

Tyson reports Monday, Nov 16, before the open. It is a $21 billion company, but its report reads two of the four fuels behind this year's inflation in one print: immigration, because meatpacking lines lean on immigrant workers, and taxes, because tariff policy sets the price of the imported beef that fills the gap when U.S. herds shrink. War and AI are the other two. When the shopper pays more and the packer still loses, the cause is supply, and a Fed hike doesn't grow cattle or staff a plant.

That gap, dearer beef and a losing packer, is a stress test. For families with seven figures invested, food inflation that outlasts a Fed hike hits bonds and stocks together. Would your plan hold? A Trefis partner firm can test it in a free 30-minute call.

So the read-through runs to prices, not to grocery stocks. Grocers can pass costs on, so your bill moves more than their stocks do. And Tyson's print matters more than usual: because October 2025 prices were never collected during the shutdown, the government could not publish a 12-month food inflation rate for October.

Which Number Decides It?

The fiscal 2027 beef outlook. Another loss near the $625-775 million guided for fiscal 2026 says the cattle shortage, and dearer beef, run through 2027. A sharply smaller loss says the worst of beef inflation is near its end. Also listen for chicken, guided to $1.85-1.95 billion of profit, and for any word on plant staffing and tariffs.

title: Walmart Inc. (WMT) is Attracting Investor Attention: Here is What You Should Know

Walmart Inc. (WMT) is Attracting Investor Attention: Here is What You Should Know
Zacks Equity Research
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST 5 min read
WMT
^GSPC
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Walmart (WMT) has recently been on Zacks.com's list of the most searched stocks. Therefore, you might want to consider some of the key factors that could influence the stock's performance in the near future.

Over the past month, shares of this world's largest retailer have returned +7.1%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -2.6% change. During this period, the Zacks Retail - Supermarkets industry, which Walmart falls in, has gained 11.6%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?

While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.

Earnings Estimate Revisions

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

Walmart is expected to post earnings of $0.64 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +3.2%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed -0.2%.

The consensus earnings estimate of $2.88 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +9.1%. This estimate has changed +0.1% over the last 30 days.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $3.22 indicates a change of +12% from what Walmart is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +0.1%.

Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Walmart is rated Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).

Key Points

Interested in BUDA? Here are five stocks we like better.

Record Q3 revenue reached $5.2 million, up 64% year over year, driven by 23% same-store sales growth, broader retail distribution and the refrigerated dressings business. Net income was about $866,000, roughly flat year over year, while adjusted EBITDA rose 35% to $1.3 million.

Buda Juice expanded its retail footprint from about 350 to 600 stores, including its first full quarter of Buda Fresh distribution at Walmart. It plans to move refrigerated dressings production to its Dallas plant in Q1 2027, which management expects to improve efficiency and reduce co-packing costs.

Gross margin fell to 40.8% from 44.5% a year earlier, largely due to dressings co-packing and higher diesel costs, but improved 417 basis points sequentially. The company ended September with $19.3 million in cash, no debt and an undrawn $3 million credit facility.

BUDA (NYSEAMERICAN:BUDA), the company behind Buda Juice, reported record third-quarter 2026 revenue of $5.2 million, up 64% from a year earlier, as stronger sales at existing stores, expanded retail distribution and a new refrigerated dressings business contributed to growth.

Same-store sales in the company's core beverage business increased 23% year over year, while net income was approximately $866,000, or $0.07 per share, essentially flat with the prior-year quarter. Net income rose 84% from the second quarter.

→ 3 Stocks Wall Street Likes More Than the Market Does

Co-founder and CEO Horatio Lonsdale-Hands said the same-store result indicated that consumers familiar with the company's products were buying more. He identified sales velocity at existing stores, new distribution and additional product lines as Buda Juice's three principal growth engines.

Margins improve sequentially

Gross profit rose 51% to $2.1 million, but gross margin declined to 40.8% from 44.5% a year earlier. Chief Financial Officer Clint Bowers said the year-over-year decline primarily reflected interim co-packing costs for refrigerated dressings and higher diesel fuel costs.

→ Keeping AI Cool: AAON Rides the AI Heatwave to Record Growth

Gross margin improved by 417 basis points from the second quarter. Bowers said the normalization of elevated lime and other produce costs was the largest factor in the sequential improvement, while Lonsdale-Hands pointed to efficiencies from higher volume.

Operating expenses rose to $1.1 million, or 21.7% of revenue, from $0.5 million, or 17% of revenue, a year earlier. Bowers attributed the increase primarily to public-company costs and non-cash stock-based compensation, as well as higher distribution costs associated with diesel prices. He noted that Buda Juice did not record federal income tax or stock-based compensation expenses in the third quarter of 2025.

title: Better Dividend Stock for Retirees: Home Depot vs. Walmart

Better Dividend Stock for Retirees: Home Depot vs. Walmart ©@Erik Gonzalez via Canva
Key Takeaways

Home Depot (HD:NYSE) yields 2.8% and Walmart (WMT:NASDAQ) yields 0.8%, so $10,000 pays $280 a year in Home Depot dividends against $80 from Walmart.

Free cash flow covers both dividends, with cash dividend payout ratios of 61% at Home Depot and 57% at Walmart over the latest twelve months.

Walmart's business and its dividend are growing faster right now, while Home Depot's bigger projects remain under pressure from a frozen housing market.

Home Depot trades at 22x forward earnings, right at its five-year average, against 42x for Walmart.

Any retiree hunting for dividend income from the stores they already shop at is going to look hard at Home Depot and Walmart. This fall, the two gave income investors very different things to weigh.

Home Depot's stock sat near 52-week lows in early October as weak housing turnover weighed on bigger projects. It then jumped 6.5% on Nov. 4 after Democrats won control of the House and Senate, as investors bet on housing-affordability policy and lower Treasury yields.

The board hasn't touched the dividend: on Aug. 20, it declared a $2.33 quarterly payout, Home Depot's 158th straight quarter of cash dividends.

Walmart, meanwhile, raised its full-year guidance in August on 23% growth in global e-commerce sales. So which one is the better bet for a retiree who wants a check they can count on?

Source: TIKR, Nov. 9, 2026; annual dividend from StockAnalysis. TTM to Aug. 2, 2026 (Home Depot) and July 31, 2026 (Walmart).

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

Home Depot pays more from a slower business

Home Depot's sales rose 5.7% to $47.9 billion in its Q2, ended Aug. 2, 2026. But comparable sales grew just 1.7%, and customer transactions fell 1.0% as bigger projects stayed on hold.

On the Q1 call in May, CEO Edward Decker said, "We're not looking at a marked improvement in underlying demand." Home Depot guides for adjusted EPS to grow anywhere from flat to 4% this fiscal year.

The dividend has grown faster than the cash behind it. From the year ended January 2017 to the year ended January 2026, dividends paid rose from $3.40 billion to $9.15 billion, while free cash flow grew from $8.16 billion to $12.7 billion:

Home Depot (HD): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2017-2026 (years to January) (TIKR)

Its cash dividend payout ratio climbed from 39% in the year ended January 2021 to a heavy 72% in the year ended January 2026, when free cash flow fell from $16.3 billion the year before.
